stops.name: Nanchang, the memory palace for Governor Lu
stops.campa: For the governor of Jiangxi, Lu Wan'gai, and his three sons preparing for the examinations, Ricci writes the Xiguo Jifa, a short treatise on the Western art of memory: build a palace of imagined rooms in the mind, he teaches, set a vivid image in each, walk it in order, and nothing so lodged is ever lost. He tells his superior that Chinese characters seem made on purpose for such a method. The governor's sons are delighted; the treatise, and the idea of a mind built like architecture, will pass down through Chinese letters long after its author is gone.

stops.name: Beijing, the shut gate
stops.campa: Riding a reputation now well ahead of him, Ricci reaches Peking for the first time, brought north by a sympathetic official hoping to present him at court. But the war with Japan over Korea still poisons the air against foreigners near the throne; no audience is granted, and after two idle months of waiting on a favor that never comes, he turns south again, disappointed but unharmed, telling his brethren that the empire's center remains, for now, closed to him exactly as it was three years before at Nanjing.

stops.name: Nanjing, the debate with the monk Xuelang
stops.campa: Returned to Nanjing in February, tolerated now in the city that once ordered him out within days, Ricci is drawn into a public dinner-table debate with the eminent Buddhist master Xuelang Hong'en before an audience of the southern capital's literati. Where the monk argues for the void and the illusory nature of the created world, Ricci argues, in the Confucian idiom he has spent fifteen years mastering, for a single eternal Creator and a real, ordered cosmos; the room, by every account he leaves us, sides with the foreigner. The monks of Nanjing will answer him in print for a generation afterward.

stops.name: Nanjing, Xu Guangqi and the road north again
stops.campa: Xu Guangqi, a Jiangsu scholar on his way to the examinations, seeks Ricci out in Nanjing and finds in him a mind as exacting as his own; the friendship formed this winter will outlast Ricci himself and carry his mathematics and his doctrine deep into the Ming bureaucracy. Within months Ricci sets out for Peking a third time, now with imperial tribute in hand, gifts assembled over years for exactly this approach: clocks, a keyboard instrument, paintings of Christ and the Virgin, a jeweled cross, and an atlas of the world he himself has drawn and redrawn.

stops.name: Tianjin, detained by the eunuch Ma Tang
stops.campa: At Tianjin, the river port that guards the last approach to the capital, the eunuch Ma Tang, who controls the customs and means to broker the foreigners' entry for his own profit, seizes Ricci's party and holds them for months, the tribute gifts impounded and his own fate uncertain. It is the tightest passage of the whole ascent, resolved only when Ma Tang, having examined the clocks and grasped that only Ricci can keep them running, sends word to the palace that the foreign gifts, and their keeper, had best be brought in after all.

stops.name: Beijing, entry at last
stops.campa: Ricci enters Peking as a bearer of tribute to the Wanli Emperor, the first Westerner given passage into the Forbidden City's outer precincts on this footing. Nineteen years after Macau, three failed approaches behind him, he stands at last inside the wall he has spent two decades of instruments, maps, mathematics and scholar's silk maneuvering to cross. The emperor, famously reclusive, will never grant him a personal audience in the nine years left to him; but the gifts are accepted, and that acceptance alone is the door held open.

stops.name: Beijing, the clocks laid before the Dragon Throne
stops.campa: Among the tribute Ricci presents are two European clocks, one large enough to chime the hours on its own, a keyboard instrument he calls the gravicembolo, paintings of Christ and the Virgin, a breviary, a jeweled crucifix, and his own world map. The emperor is enchanted above all by the striking clock, orders a tower built for the larger one within the palace, and sets eunuchs to learn the keyboard from Ricci's colleague Diego de Pantoja; after a month's teaching they can barely play one air through. Wanli never receives Ricci in person, but keeps him, paid and housed, for this machinery's sake alone.

stops.name: Beijing, a stipend, a house, a church
stops.campa: The court grants Ricci an official stipend and leave to remain in the capital, an unprecedented standing for a foreign priest, lodging him where the palace eunuchs can reach him for the clocks. Four years on he buys a house near the Xuanwu Gate, ground that will grow, long after him, into the Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception. From this city he will not move again. The strategy begun at Zhaoqing eighteen years before, enter through curiosity, remain through utility, convert through friendship, has reached the one capital it was always aimed at, and the slower work of the doctrine can begin in earnest.

stops.name: Beijing, the Kunyu Wanguo Quantu for the emperor
stops.campa: At the request of the court, Ricci and the scholar Li Zhizao print a great world map in six panels of mulberry paper, the Kunyu Wanguo Quantu, the finished descendant of the sheet he first drew at Zhaoqing eighteen years before. He shifts the central meridian so that China, no longer crowded to the eastern edge as European projections leave it, sits nearer the middle of the sheet, a courtesy to the empire's own sense of its place, and annotates every ocean and continent, Florida rendered as the Land of Flowers, in careful, respectful Chinese prose.
stops.quote: It offers testimony to the supreme goodness, greatness and unity of Him who controls heaven and earth.
stops.quote_source: Ricci, annotation on the Kunyu Wanguo Quantu (1602)

stops.name: Nanjing, Xu Guangqi is baptized Paul
stops.campa: Xu Guangqi, the Jiangsu scholar who sought Ricci out in Nanjing three years before, returns to the mission house there and is baptized Paul by Father Joao da Rocha. Ricci, far north in Peking, is not present and learns of it by letter. It is the mission's most consequential conversion. Where Qu Taisu opened the mandarin circles of the south, Xu Guangqi will open the machinery of the state itself, rising to Grand Secretary and shielding the Jesuits at court for the rest of his long career; the friendship, already years old, is about to become the mission's most lasting written work.

stops.name: Beijing, the True Meaning of the Lord of Heaven
stops.campa: Ricci publishes the Tianzhu Shiyi, the True Meaning of the Lord of Heaven, cast as a dialogue between a Chinese scholar and a Western one, arguing the existence of one Creator God from reason and from the oldest Confucian classics themselves, which he reads as preserving a memory of the true God that later commentators buried under Buddhist and Neo-Confucian accretion. The book is reprinted repeatedly in his lifetime and after, read by emperors and hostile critics alike, and remains for two centuries the single most influential work of Christian apologetics written in the Chinese language.

stops.name: Beijing, the Elements of Euclid rendered into Chinese
stops.campa: Ricci dictates and Xu Guangqi transcribes the Jihe Yuanben, the first six books of Euclid's Elements in Chinese, from the Latin edition their common teacher Clavius annotated in Rome thirty years before. Xu, laboring over terms with no precedent in the language, coins the words for point, line, plane and parallel that Chinese mathematics still uses. The two men meet through a bitter Peking winter to finish it: Clavius's classroom, entire, delivered forty years on to the other end of the earth, the deductive method Ricci once learned as a boy now argued step by step in literary Chinese.
